develop an ex-vivo autologous stem-cell editing programme, comparing direct repair and fetal-hemoglobin-reactivation targets before clinical commitment

Target fetal-hemoglobin reactivation via genetic disruption of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer using Cas9-mediated non-homologous end-joining, in autologous CD34+ HSPCs, rather than attempting direct beta-globin mutation repair or other individual fetal-hemoglobin-regulatory genes.

Target the BCL11A erythroid-lineage enhancer (specifically its GATA1-binding region) in the intronic regulatory element of BCL11A, using programmable Cas9 editing in autologous CD34+ HSPCs ex vivo, to downregulate BCL11A in erythroid cells and thereby reactivate fetal hemoglobin, followed by myeloablative conditioning and re-infusion.

Prioritize targeted disruption of a fetal-hemoglobin (HbF) repressor element—specifically the BCL11A erythroid enhancer in the +58 kb intronic region—in autologous CD34+ HSPCs via Cas9, inducing HbF upregulation rather than direct beta-globin mutation repair. This route is selected because it leverages a validated enhancer/repressor biology axis, minimizes the cleavage-site sequence diversity/variant-correction burden carried by direct repair, and is assessable end-to-end through existing fetal-hemoglobin quantification and colony-forming assays.

candidate-target comparison followed by ex-vivo stem-cell editing with molecular and off-target assays, prioritizing a fetal-hemoglobin upregulation strategy (e.g., disrupting a repressive regulatory element in the gamma-globin promoter region) versus direct beta-globin mutation repair as parallel arms in an early functional-editing preclinical screen.
